--- Summary ---
Redwood and DataForge walked through recent instability: OOMs on long sequence runs (~800-1200 tokens), intermittent CUDA "context lost" and driver messages, and timeouts in the VPC deployment. Focus on root causes: model KV cache behavior, batch sizing, quantization profiles, pinned host memory, cudaMalloc failures and fragmentation, and how Redwood's retry semantics interact with idempotency and latency SLOs.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with me is Luis, our SE, and Jared on SRE. could you all do quick intros?
[00:10] Priya Nair: sure, priya here, engineering manager for the inference team at DataForge. we've been seeing intermittent OOMs on our VPC deployment with long sequences, and want to understand why and figure out a plan.
[00:22] Ben Ortiz: ben, infra lead. i run the nodes in our private subnet, we've got 8xA100s per rack, but we've seen cuda driver error spikes and sometimes the node reboots, or the container dies with cudaMalloc failed.
[00:34] Sofia Lopez: sofia from security/compliance - i'll just be listening for any network/VPC compliance implications.
[00:40] Luis Alvarez: thanks - quick high level, we've looked at the traces you sent; there are a few patterns: 1) memory blow-ups at long sequence lengths where kv cache isn't being reused optimally, 2) fragmentation leading to cudaMalloc failing even when aggregate free memory looks ok, and 3) timeouts triggered by our client-side retry semantics which can exacerbate load.
[01:05] Ben Ortiz: can you expand on the fragmentation bit? we thought if we had enough free mem it shouldn't OOM.
[01:12] Luis Alvarez: yeah so this is common with long-running pinned allocations and mixed batch sizes. when you do a lot of small ephemeral allocations plus large KV cache allocations, the allocator (cuda + libcudnn) can fragment. the OS-level free looks ok but contiguous chunk to satisfy a big allocation isn't available. also cuda context resets show up as driver messages - sometimes that looks like "CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY" followed by "context lost".
[01:40] Jared Kim: i'll add, on our side we've seen patterns where quantized kernels have slightly different memory patterns; int8/4bit can reduce peak but sometimes increase temporary workspace allocations for certain fused kernels during attention, so there's a tradeoff.
[02:00] Priya Nair: hmm we are using a 4-bit quant profile for cost savings. maybe that changed behavior. we also saw timeouts after about 20 seconds on requests that hit a fallback in the model routing.
[02:14] Luis Alvarez: fallback + retries is important: client SDK has exponential backoff by default, but if retries aren't idempotent (e.g., changing session state, or re-attaching a KV cache) you can cause duplicate work and additional memory pressure. We recommend idempotent request markers and server-side dedup where possible.
[02:35] Ben Ortiz: are there Redwood config knobs to reduce fragmentation or control allocation behavior?
[02:40] Luis Alvarez: yes, a few we discussed: pre-allocating large GPU arenas, setting CUDA_CACHEPATH/persisted kernels, using our pinned host memory fallback (if you enable host staging the device peaks are lower but latency might go up a bit), and controlling batch sizes and batch timeouts so you don't accumulate lots of in-flight KV caches.
[03:05] Priya Nair: pinned host memory fallback - is that safe in a VPC environment? does it affect isolation?
[03:12] Jared Kim: it's safe - it's just a memory staging strategy, no cross-tenant sharing. in private deployments you control the nodes, and we don't colocate other customers. it will increase host memory usage though.
[03:25] Sofia Lopez: any compliance or audit log impacts from those changes?
[03:29] Maya Chen: no, those are local runtime flags. bigger compliance items are around audit logs and key management for Private - we'll share the SOC2 doc and our VPC deployment guide after the call.
[03:40] Ben Ortiz: thank you.
[03:44] [05:00] Luis Alvarez: i want to show a small diagram of the KV cache lifecycle - describe how prefix caching and eviction works, but i'm not screen sharing in this transcript. core point: if you pin multiple sessions and don't evict or use a shared prefix cache, memory accumulates; the eviction policy is LRU but it can be tuned by retention window and max-kv-bytes.
[05:26] Priya Nair: our service pins sessions for multi-turn chat for 30 minutes. could that be the cause?
[05:33] Luis Alvarez: yes, thirty minutes with large sequence lengths can cause retained KV to grow across many users. consider reducing retention or using per-route shorter retention for high-memory models. also enabling shared prefix cache for similar prompts can greatly reduce duplicate KV.
[05:50] Ben Ortiz: how does batching factor in? we try to batch to increase throughput.
[05:56] Luis Alvarez: batching is great for throughput but also increases transient memory: if your batch target is 8 and you have variable sequence lengths, the runtime pads and may allocate max_seq * batch_size for some buffers. continuous batching mitigates but you need good packing policies and max tokens per batch. lowering max batch size or using dynamic padding can help.
[06:22] Priya Nair: we do dynamic padding already but still see peaks. any quick flags we can flip?
[06:28] Luis Alvarez: set a hard cap on max_batch_tokens, reduce batching window (so you don't accumulate too many requests waiting), or use our per-route batching policy to prioritize latency-sensitive routes with smaller batch sizes.
[06:40] [10:12] Ben Ortiz: about the CUDA driver errors - our node logs show: "NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:65:00): 31, ..." and then container OOM. is that a driver bug or our code?
[10:25] Jared Kim: Xid 31 often points to illegal memory access from the kernel - could be due to bad kernels (custom fused kernels), or memory corruption when multiple processes share the GPU. we also see a class of Xid associated with running out of VRAM during large workspace allocations. important to capture the dmesg, nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY and the container runtime logs.
[10:48] Luis Alvarez: also check GPU persistence mode and driver versions - some driver-model combos had regressions. we saw one case where newer driver + certain libcudnn caused larger workspace. we've got a compatibility matrix we'll share.
[11:05] Priya Nair: we'll pull those logs. you mentioned kernel fusion - are those Redwood kernels or model-lib kernels?
[11:12] Luis Alvarez: a mix. Redwood runtime selects optimized kernels; sometimes it will use vendor fused kernels or fall back to more generic ones. quantization sometimes triggers a fused kernel path that increases temporary workspace. that's why we profile both int8 and fp16 for your workload.
[11:28] Priya Nair: how about retries - we've seen many 504s and client retries that made load worse. what do you recommend for retry limits?
[11:36] Maya Chen: recommended pattern: short client timeout (so latency SLO met), but moderate retry cap with exponential backoff and jitter. on the server we support idempotency keys; combine that with circuit-breakers so repeated failures don't overload the service. for private deployments you can configure retry policies in the ingress/router.
[12:00] Ben Ortiz: what about request types that mutate state, like streaming sessions where we append to conversation? retries could duplicate tokens.
[12:09] Luis Alvarez: exactly - for session mutation we require idempotency markers per request or avoid automatic client retries. another pattern: separate append operations from generation and make append explicit with safe-write semantics.
[12:23] [15:00] Priya Nair: can you explain Redwood's retry semantics in the Dedicated/private runtime? are retries synchronous and do they create new goroutines/processes?
[15:10] Jared Kim: retries are handled by the client and the front-end router; the router will not automatically replay a request without an idempotency key. the server has a short-lived in-flight cache to dedupe duplicate requests within a very short window. for cases where a backend times out but the generator actually completes, we expose an async result store so clients can fetch answers without re-submitting.
[15:35] Ben Ortiz: async result store - does that persist to disk? any encryption concerns?
[15:40] Maya Chen: yes it writes to ephemeral storage encrypted with KMS in Private, and retention is configurable. we'll include the encryption + KMS details in the VPC doc.
[15:52] [18:30] Luis Alvarez: looking at the traces you provided, one pattern stood out: a mix of a high variance in sequence length and a small number of very large sequences causes the scheduler to pack small ones and then suddenly accept a 1k token request that forces large temporary allocations. our runtime has an admission control knob that rejects huge requests when memory headroom below threshold. you can tune that threshold.
[19:05] Priya Nair: we would prefer not to reject big requests; we need to support long conversations. what are mitigation options?
[19:13] Luis Alvarez: options: 1) enable streaming/partial token generation to reduce peak (emit earlier tokens as produced), 2) share KV cache across similar sessions, 3) use quantization to reduce per-token bytes (but verify workspace impact), 4) provision Dedicated capacity sized for your 95th percentile sequences.
[19:38] Ben Ortiz: for Dedicated, what's the recommended GPU type and config? we currently run A100 40GB; should we move to 80GB?
[19:46] Jared Kim: 80GB reduces fragmentation pressure for very large KV, but it's also more expensive. Another approach is multi-GPU sharding (tensor/model parallelism) if you hit single-GPU limits, but that increases complexity. For many customers, 40GB with careful packing, pre-alloc arenas, and host staging has been sufficient. We'll give an explicit sizing guidance after seeing your bench results.
[20:12] [22:00] Priya Nair: what about NCCL issues or network errors in VPC leading to timeouts?
[22:08] Luis Alvarez: if you do multi-node sharding, NCCL and the fabric matter - packet drops or high jitter can cause hangs and timeouts. For single-node Dedicated, it's less of a factor. On VPC we recommend accelerated networking, MTU tuning, and avoiding ephemeral NAT for GPU nodes because SNAT can introduce jitter.
[22:34] Ben Ortiz: our nodes are behind a NAT gateway. could that be a problem?
[22:38] Jared Kim: possibly, if your traffic crosses the NAT for internal RPCs. check routing so intra-cluster control traffic stays local.
[22:46] [25:00] Priya Nair: some of our errors were only in the VPC staging env, not in the cloud-hosted Redwood test. could it be a kernel config?
[25:07] Luis Alvarez: yes kernel and driver config diffs can explain behavior. things to check: oom_kill settings, transparent huge pages, memory cgroup config, and the exact NVIDIA driver and CUDA versions. we will send a diagnostic checklist.
[25:26] Ben Ortiz: please also include dmesg parse examples.
[25:29] Luis Alvarez: yes will do.
[25:33] [28:00] Priya Nair: quantization - you said some fused kernels have higher workspace. any heuristic to predict this?
[28:08] Luis Alvarez: our profiling tool will run representative prompts and report workspace and peak mem for fp16, int8, and 4-bit. for many transformer blocks int8 reduces peak, but fused attention/kv ops may allocate extra scratch. run the profiler. Luis: i'll share a CSV of the prof.
[28:30] Ben Ortiz: is there any runtime switch to force non-fused kernels for stability?
[28:35] Luis Alvarez: yes you can disable fast fused kernels in runtime flags; that increases latency a bit but reduces peak workspace variability. it's a common stability mitigation.
[28:45] [32:15] Priya Nair: about observability - we want to correlate Prometheus metrics, logs, and GPU traces. what's Redwood's recommendation?
[32:23] Maya Chen: we have per-route metrics (token/sec, latency p50/p95, gpu_mem_used) exported to Prometheus, and we can push structured trace spans to your tracing stack. We'll provide mapping docs. Include GPU metrics (nvidia-smi telemetry) and dmesg for kernel errors.
[32:45] Sofia Lopez: does Redwood keep logs in private deployments? retention policy?
[32:50] Maya Chen: for Private, the control plane can be configured to forward logs to your chosen S3/stack, retention is configurable, and all logs can be encrypted with customer KMS. we'll include the retention options.
[33:05] [36:00] Ben Ortiz: one more question on retries: if a request times out client-side but the server later completes, how do we avoid lost results?
[36:10] Luis Alvarez: two patterns: 1) async result store + polling/long-poll, 2) idempotency key + server dedupe that returns completed result if it's already processed. we recommend putting an idempotency key on each submission and short polling the async store for long runs.
[36:32] Priya Nair: will that increase memory? you'd store results somewhere transiently.
[36:37] Jared Kim: it's disk backed and ephemeral; it's tuned to not keep large results long. encryption with KMS is used. It adds storage cost but avoids dangerous retry storms.
[36:50] [40:00] Luis Alvarez: to recap mitigation checklist: - collect and send dmesg, nvidia-smi, container logs - run our profiling harness on representative prompts for fp16/int8/4-bit - try host staging/pinned host memory if you need immediate relief - consider reducing KV retention or enabling shared prefix cache - tune batching windows and max_batch_tokens - enable idempotency keys and async result store for long-running requests
[40:34] Priya Nair: ok that sounds actionable.
[40:38] Ben Ortiz: timeline - we can run the bench this week.
[40:42] Maya Chen: perfect. we'll send the log script and bench harness now; expecting initial results early next week.
[40:50] [45:00] Sofia Lopez: small note, for SOC2 + VPC we need details on network segmentation and audit logs.
[45:08] Maya Chen: noted, i'll include that in the doc pack.
[45:12] [49:00] Priya Nair: any known issues with specific driver versions? we saw different behavior between 535.x and 545.x series.
[49:10] Luis Alvarez: yes there were some regressions in 545.x for certain fused kernels; we'll include our compatibility matrix (driver/CUDA/cudnn/runtime) in the notes.
[49:28] Ben Ortiz: okay thanks that's helpful.
[49:33] [52:30] Maya Chen: let's confirm next steps: we'll send: bench harness, log collection script, SOC2/VPC doc, and initial pricing for a Dedicated pilot. DataForge will run bench and upload logs, then we'll huddle next week.
[52:50] Priya Nair: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[52:55] Ben Ortiz: thanks.
